# pacfwei

**Partial autocorrelation for multivariate time series.**

`pacfwei` provides `pacf_wei()`, which implements the multivariate partial
autocorrelation fucntion described by Wei (2006). It offers a fast C implementation and
an R implementation of the same forward/backward recursion, with C as the
default. Both return standard `acf` objects for printing, plotting, and
extracting coefficients.

## Installation

Install the unpacked source directory from its parent folder:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("pacfwei", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```

A compiler toolchain is required to install from source, including compatible
Rtools on Windows. The installed package depends only on R's `stats` and
`graphics` packages; the C code uses R's BLAS and LAPACK libraries.

## Getting started

The package includes the annual Lydia Pinkham advertising and sales data used
in Wei's multivariate example. First-difference both series before computing
the partial autocorrelations:

```{r pinkham}
library(pacfwei)
data("pinkham", package = "pacfwei")

# The supplied dataset is a two-column data frame; add annual time metadata.
pinkham_ts <- ts(pinkham, start = 1907, frequency = 1)
changes <- diff(pinkham_ts)

pc <- pacf_wei(changes, lag.max = 6, plot = FALSE)
round(pc$acf[1:2, , ], 3)
```

Use the usual `acf` plotting method to display all component pairs:

```{r pinkham-pacf}
plot(pc)
```

See `?pinkham` for the data format and sources, and `?pacf_wei` for the full
mathematical definition and recursion.

## Choosing an implementation

```{r implementations}
pr <- pacf_wei(changes, lag.max = 6, plot = FALSE, method = "R")
isTRUE(all.equal(pc$acf, pr$acf, tolerance = 1e-10))
```

Use `method = "C"` (the default) or `method = "R"`. Name this argument
explicitly because it follows `...` in the function signature. The methods
estimate the same quantity; small floating-point differences are possible.
Univariate inputs use `stats::pacf()` with either method.

## What is being estimated?

At lag $s$, project the vector observations $Z_{t+s}$ and $Z_t$ on all the
intervening vectors $Z_{t+1},\ldots,Z_{t+s-1}$. Let $u$ and $v$ be the
residual vectors at times $t+s$ and $t$, respectively. The returned entry is

$$
P_R(s)_{ij} =
\frac{Cov(u_i,v_j)}
{\sqrt{Var(u_i)Var(v_j)}}.
$$

These are componentwise residual correlations. They do not additionally
condition on the other components at time $t$ or $t+s$. Entries are bounded
by one in absolute value, up to numerical roundoff, whenever the required
residual variances and regression systems are well defined.

The coefficient array `pc$acf` has dimensions $p \times m \times m$, where
$p$ is the maximum lag and $m$ is the number of components. Its axes index
lag, component at time $t+s$, and component at time $t$, following R's
positive-lag convention. A lag matrix need not be symmetric. Wei uses the transposed
orientation; obtain it with `aperm(pc$acf, c(1, 3, 2))`.

For multivariate input, `stats::pacf()` in the R version for which this package
was developed returns partial autoregression coefficients, which can exceed
one in magnitude. Those coefficients differ from the residual correlations
computed here. Loading `pacfwei` leaves `stats::pacf()` unchanged.

## Inputs and numerical behavior

- Supply a numeric vector, matrix, data frame, or time series. Rows are
  observations and columns are components.
- Use `plot = FALSE` to return the result without drawing a plot. Extract
  coefficients with `$acf`; with `plot = TRUE`, the result is returned invisibly.
- Multivariate data must be finite, with positive marginal variances after
  `na.action` is applied. The default `stats::na.fail` rejects missing values.
- For multivariate input with $n$ observations and $m$ components, the default
  maximum lag is `floor(10 * log10(n / m))`. The lag must be at least one and
  is capped at $n - 1$; set it explicitly when necessary.
- Both implementations use centered sample covariances with denominator $n$
  and rescale columns internally to improve numerical conditioning.
  Singular regression systems produce an error. Short samples with many
  components or large lag orders can fail; neither method regularizes the
  covariance matrices or clips the correlations.

## References

Wei, W. W. S. (2006). *Time Series Analysis: Univariate and Multivariate
Methods*, second edition. Pearson Prentice Hall. Section 16.5.3,
pp. 408-414, defines the partial autocorrelations and recursion;
Section 16.7 illustrates them with the Lydia Pinkham data.

Palda, K. S. (1965). The Measurement of Cumulative Advertising Effects.
*The Journal of Business*, *38*(2), 162–179.
[http://www.jstor.org/stable/2350780](http://www.jstor.org/stable/2350780)
